name: Anne Llewellyn Barstow
primary_institution: State University of New York (College at Old Westbury)
specialization: Feminist analysis of European witch-hunts; gender and misogyny in prosecution

major_works.title: Witchcraze: A New History of the European Witch Hunts
major_works.significance: Argued that the European witch-hunts were fundamentally misogynist in motivation and effect; brought feminist analysis to wide popular and scholarly audience

major_works.title: Married Priests and the Reforming Papacy
major_works.significance: Earlier work on gender and clerical culture in medieval church

core_argument: The European witch-hunts were fundamentally an attack on women, motivated by misogyny rooted in clerical culture and patriarchal social structures. The disproportionate targeting of women — approximately 80% of the accused in most regions — reflects not coincidence but systematic fear and hatred of female power, sexuality, and autonomy. Witch-hunting was gendered violence at a mass scale.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Cross-regional prosecution statistics; demonological texts with misogynist content; trial records showing gender of accused
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Gender distribution of accused; misogynist themes in demonological literature; relationship between clerical celibacy culture and witch-hunting
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Statistical gender analysis of prosecution records; textual analysis of demonological misogyny
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Patriarchal structural: misogynist ideology as primary driver of gendered prosecution

key_contributions.claim: The systematic targeting of women in witch prosecutions constitutes a form of gendered violence comparable to modern gender-based persecution
key_contributions.implication: Historical witch-hunting should be understood in feminist frameworks of structural violence

key_contributions.claim: The misogynist ideology embedded in clerical culture, especially the Malleus Maleficarum's explicit woman-hatred, directly shaped prosecution patterns
key_contributions.implication: Intellectual history of demonological misogyny is inseparable from the gendered pattern of prosecutions

key_contributions.claim: Statistical evidence of female predominance among the accused is itself an argument for gender as primary explanatory category
key_contributions.implication: Any adequate explanation of witch-hunting must account for the gender disparity

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Second-wave feminist historiography; women's history movement; Mary Daly's theological feminist analysis
criticisms: Midelfort and others show that large panics had substantially higher male representation, complicating simple misogyny thesis
Briggs argues that community-level evidence shows women accusing women, not patriarchal persecution from above
Levack argues multi-causal model is better supported by regional variation than single-cause gender explanation
Some historians argue the misogyny thesis conflates different regional and temporal patterns
Roper accepted gender analysis but replaced misogyny with a more nuanced psychoanalytic account of gender dynamics

historiographical_significance: Barstow's work elevated gender to the center of witchcraft historiography and brought feminist analysis to a wide audience. While her strong misogyny thesis has been qualified by subsequent regional scholarship, she established the non-negotiability of gender as an analytical category in any serious account of European witch-hunting. Her work stimulated productive debate that refined the field's understanding of gender dynamics.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
